title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction:
Context: the memoir minimizes or maximizes ∫ w(v) √(dx²+dy²+dz²) over space curves, where v = √(x²+y²+z²) is the distance from a fixed point O and w is an arbitrary function. In §§1–42 Euler solved this by a long three-dimensional computation. That computation showed the extremal lies in a plane through O and gave its polar equation. On this page (§43–44) he remarks that the result was foreseeable. The integrand depends only on the radial distance and the arc element, so the problem is really two-dimensional. It can be posed as a plane problem: find a curve around a centre C that extremizes ∫ w(v) ds.

He then uses polar coordinates. He calls the radius x and the polar angle y (measured from a fixed line CD), so ds = √(dx² + x² dy²). With dy = p dx the functional becomes ∫ w(x) √(1+p²x²) dx, i.e. V = w√(1+p²x²). Writing dV = M dx + N dy + P dp, he notes that y is absent, so N = 0 and P = w x² p/√(1+p²x²). On the next page the Euler equation N dx = dP gives the first integral P = const.

In modern terms: the angle is a cyclic coordinate, and the conserved momentum is w(r) r² θ'/√(1+r²θ'²) = w(r) r sin ψ = c, where ψ is the angle between the curve and the radius vector. This is the Bouguer/Clairaut-type invariant for rays in a spherically symmetric medium, i.e. conservation of angular momentum. Solving gives θ = ∫ c dr / (r√(w²r² − c²)), matching the earlier laborious result with x→v, y→φ. The methodological moral Euler draws is that a suitable transformation turns a hard problem into an easy one.
errors: The printed formula ∫w√(∂x²+yy∂y²) is a misprint for ∫w√(∂x²+xx∂y²); the line just before correctly has ∂s=√(∂x²+xx∂y²). The image confirms 'yy' is in the original print.
On the next page '∂y = ∫ c∂x/(x√(wwx²−cc))' should read 'y = ∫ …' (or ∂y = c∂x/…, without the integral sign).

Minor: the reduction to a plane problem is asserted from the structure of the integrand rather than proved. One needs the symmetry argument (rotational invariance about O implies a planar extremal through O, since angular momentum is conserved and its direction fixed). Euler's own earlier solution supplies this, so it is not a real gap.

ideas.what: Reduction of a rotationally invariant 3D variational problem ∫w(|x|)ds to a planar problem, because the extremal lies in a plane through the centre
ideas.modern_name: Symmetry reduction / conservation of angular momentum vector (central-force planarity)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Newton for central forces; formalized via Noether, 1918)
ideas.where_published: This memoir E740; analogous central-force planarity arguments appear throughout Euler's mechanics

ideas.what: Polar-coordinate Euler–Lagrange equation with cyclic angle giving the first integral w r² θ'/√(1+r²θ'²) = c
ideas.modern_name: Cyclic coordinate first integral; Bouguer's/Clairaut's relation n r sin ψ = const for rays in spherically stratified media
ideas.usually_credited_to: Bouguer (atmospheric refraction, 1729/1749); Clairaut (geodesics on surfaces of revolution, 1733); Euler's Methodus inveniendi (1744) for the general rule that an absent variable gives P = const
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi lineas curvas (E65, 1744), cases where N = 0; Euler's refraction papers

ideas.what: Explicit quadrature θ = ∫ c dr/(r√(w²r²−c²)) for extremals of ∫w(r)ds
ideas.modern_name: Ray/orbit equation in a central potential (Binet-type quadrature)
ideas.where_published: Equivalent to central-force orbit quadratures in Euler's mechanics

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a standard methodological remark plus a routine polar-coordinate application of Euler's own isoperimetric rule; the conserved quantity is the well-known Bouguer/Clairaut/angular-momentum invariant. Nothing absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: The transcription faithfully reproduces the original misprint 'yy∂y²' in ∫w√(∂x²+yy∂y²); mathematically it should be xx∂y².
Margin note 'Tab. I. Fig. 2.' belongs beside the line 'ca centrum C describenda, in qua, posita distantia CZ=v'.
